name: Witch hazel extract

lead: Witch hazel extract comes from the bark and leaves of a North American shrub and is the classic astringent toner. People with oily or blemish-prone skin use it to reduce shine and get a tighter feel with smaller-looking pores.

The chain is astringent: it is rich in tannins such as hamamelitannin, which tighten the skin surface and reduce oil feel. Native American and later settler use on swellings and external inflammations is part of its history. Published literature is laboratory work, including antibacterial studies of a standardised extract; human trials of its toner effect were not identified.

paras: Applied with a cotton pad or sprayed after cleansing, usually once or twice daily on oily areas, before serum and moisturiser. It is often combined with other oil-control steps. The tightening feel is immediate.
Traditional toner distillates are made with alcohol, which can dry or sting sensitive skin. Safety data were not reviewed in the available sources, and alcohol-free versions exist.

angle.text: Witch hazel is a classic astringent toner used by people with oily or blemish-prone skin to cut shine and get a tighter feel. Its tannins act on the skin surface, which reads as less oil and smaller-looking pores.

lead: Witch hazel extract is a preparation made from the bark and leaves of Hamamelis virginiana, a shrub native to eastern North America. It is best known as the astringent "witch hazel" sold as a skin toner, a product made by distilling the plant material in dilute alcohol [1]. People use it after cleansing to leave skin feeling tighter and fresher, with pores that look smaller and oily shine that looks reduced, and many use it on blemish-prone areas as part of an everyday routine for clearer-looking skin.

Native American peoples used preparations of the bark and leaves for swellings and external inflammations, and the remedy was adopted by early settlers in New England [1]. The plant contains tannins, including a type called hamamelitannin [1][2].
Published research on witch hazel extract is mostly laboratory work, such as antibacterial tests and chemical analyses [2][3][4][5]. No human trial of its use as a skincare toner was identified.
infobox: Tannins including hamamelitannin and gallic acid [2][3]

paras: As a toner, witch hazel is wiped across the face after washing.

The extract also appears as an ingredient in other personal-care products. Examples among patents are a facial mask pack with witch hazel at 15 percent [6], and a scalp shampoo with 18 to 20 volume percent witch hazel extract aimed at stimulating blood flow around the follicle and contracting pores [7]. In a Korean patent for a mask pack, witch hazel is part of a formulation with glycerin and hyaluronate [6].
Wikipedia also notes that the bark and leaves are made into tea for stomach upset and sore throat, citing an archived web page, and that its distillate is the base of the product Pond's Extract [1].

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Witch hazel is used for how skin looks and feels: as a toner wiped on after washing, it is meant to leave oily skin feeling tighter and cleaner, make pores look smaller and calm redness. Healthline describes witch hazel as an astringent that causes tissue to contract, potentially shrinking the apparent size of pores, and says its tannins and gallic acid are anti-inflammatory compounds that may soothe skin; the page says it is common in over-the-counter acne products and especially suited to oily skin.[8] The chain, in the words of the people who use it, runs from astringent action to a smaller-looking pore and less shine to a clearer-looking complexion.

Scalp products are a second use. A Korean patent describes a shampoo with 18 to 20 percent witch hazel extract by volume aimed at stimulating blood flow around the follicle and contracting pores on the scalp, and Healthline cites an older study of 1,373 people in which a witch hazel shampoo reduced scalp irritation.[7][8]

The species was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. Accounts cited on Wikipedia say Native Americans boiled stems into a decoction for swellings and inflammations, and that early New England settlers adopted the remedy; some commercial history statements on that page are marked as lacking citations [1]. The page also cites a 1997 Connecticut Business Journal article on which company makes witch hazel [1].
Common names include witch-hazel, American witch-hazel and beadwood [1].

Witch hazel produces gallotannins, and a metabolomic analysis profiled its gallotannin content [4]. One standardised extract used in research is described as high in phenolics, about 75% of which is hamamelitannin, with traces of gallic acid [2]. Hamamelitannin is described as inhibiting staphylococcal pathogenesis, including biofilm formation and toxin production, in laboratory studies [2][3].
A 2012 laboratory study reported that hamamelitannin was cytotoxic to colon cancer cells [1].

An in vitro study of whISOBAX, a standardised extract, found it inhibited the growth of all bacteria tested to varying degrees, with Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus species most sensitive, and enhanced the effect of antibiotics [2]. A study of a teat dip found that adding witch hazel extract raised the minimal inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations of an iodine-based dip against S. epidermidis cells up to 160-fold, and that only the extract inhibited toxin production [3].

A study on dandruff-associated microbes tested the witch hazel compound hamamelitannin alongside zinc pyrithione, ketoconazole and ciclopirox against Malassezia and Staphylococcus species; shampoos containing ketoconazole and zinc pyrithione were the most effective against Malassezia in the lab [9]. A 2022 study evaluated the extract for a prebiotic and protective effect on two Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains, reporting that at the higher tested dose growth was greater than with control [5].

Healthline lists studies from 2022 and 2024 on anti-inflammatory and anti-acne effects in human skin cells and on antioxidant activity, alongside a 2014 scalp-care paper, and states that studies are limited and more research is needed.[8] The same page says some people may experience skin irritation or allergic reactions and recommends a patch test on a small area first.[8] Distilled witch hazel is traditionally prepared in dilute alcohol, a factor that product labels and consumers often weigh when choosing a toner.[1]

No studies found. Related laboratory research includes an in vitro study of a witch hazel extract (whISOBAX) in which it inhibited aspects of staphylococcal pathogenesis and enhanced the effect of antibiotics [2], a study of witch hazel added to commercial cattle teat dips [3], a study of its prebiotic and protective effect on Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains [5], and a dandruff-microbe study of hamamelitannin [9]. None of these tested witch hazel on human skin.

Registered studies that mention witch hazel include a single-group evaluation of a cosmetic product line on acne symptoms in 36 participants (NCT06122467), which tests a product range rather than witch hazel alone.[10]

Witch hazel is a long-standing toner ingredient in drugstore skincare, and the classic distillate is prepared in dilute alcohol [1]. Wikipedia describes the plant as a pollinator species that supports many caterpillar species [1].
